Incorporating the July 2019 SLOOS, the FOMC’s mid‑cycle “insurance” cut to 1.75–2.00% looks more justified and slightly more dovish than previously assessed. Banks reported tighter standards for C&I loans and for construction and land development loans, along with tighter other terms across firm sizes and weaker demand in construction/land development—signals of emerging headwinds to business credit that align with the statement’s softness in business fixed investment and exports. By contrast, consumer credit conditions were broadly steady to supportive (unchanged demand for other consumer loans, reported willingness to lend, and unchanged standards on some government loans, with stronger demand for government loans), consistent with solid household spending. Financial stability considerations (elevated valuations, corporate leverage, nonbank intermediation) keep the tone balanced, but SLOOS tilts the policy bias a bit more accommodative at the margin. Implementation details (IOER to 1.80%, directive to keep EFFR in range, continued Treasury/agency MBS reinvestments, and a 25 bp primary credit rate cut) remain appropriate. Split dissents underscore uncertainty around r* and near‑term growth.

Adjusting for SLOOS’s tighter business credit signals, the overall assessment shifts modestly more dovish.
